headline: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh proved more hawkish than expected at his first meeting, focusing on price stability, which ultimately drove 10-year US rates lower
reasoning: Markets expected incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to be dovish, but his first meeting delivered a hawkish tone with a focus on price stability. Markets initially reacted negatively to this, but subsequently interpreted the stance as positive for long-term interest rates. As a result, 10-year US Treasury yields fell following the meeting. Taylor views this as a net positive for investors over the medium to long term.
quote: we've got a new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, and his first meeting was held in June, and it was widely expected that he would be quite dovish towards markets, but in fact, he proved to be quite hawkish. And he really focused on price stability, which markets initially took those negatively, but after a while, they came to understand that actually it's quite positive for long-term interest rates. And so, we saw the 10-year US rates fall post that first meeting.
episode_title: Mike Taylor June insights: Middle East ceasefire, new Fed Chair and the world's biggest IPO

headline: Pie Funds moderately upbeat on UK outlook as inflation eases and rate cuts expected by end of 2025

Um now as we know energy prices are coming down and so is kind of core inflation. headline: Pie Funds CIO Mike Taylor sees AI trade as fundamentally different from dot-com bubble, driven by real revenues and earnings
reasoning: Taylor acknowledges the AI trade is in full swing and drawing comparisons to the dot-com bubble, but argues the situations are materially different. He notes names like Hewlett-Packard, Dell, and Micron rising 30% in a day, reflecting genuine business momentum rather than speculative excess.
quote: The AI trade is in full swing. Um there's lots of people reminiscing to the dot-com bubble out there. Uh we don't quite feel it's the same. Um dot-com was periods where companies with no revenue were IPOing on the Nasdaq, uh and prices going to the moon. Today, we've actually got uh prices of AI hardware-related companies that are shooting up on actual revenue and actually really strong earnings. So, that's what's driving a very small segment of the market. Uh I mean, you're seeing some old favorites like Hewlett-Packard, Dell, uh Micron up 30% in a day in some cases.

headline: Matt Young argues Iran conflict and prior Russian gas cutoff have made European energy security a lasting structural theme benefiting energy infrastructure holdings
reasoning: Young notes that the property and infrastructure fund's energy infrastructure names have held up well through the Iran conflict. He argues that even after the conflict reaches equilibrium, lasting impacts will remain — particularly for Europe, which imports a significant portion of its energy. The combination of Iranian supply disruption and the prior cutoff of Russian gas has made energy security a top priority, creating a durable tailwind for holdings that facilitate energy supply into Europe.
quote: Yeah, it's held up pretty well. We have particularly our energy infrastructure names. And I think the thing that really excites me is even once we reach a equilibrium in the Iran conflict, there will still be lasting impacts. So, if you're sitting in Europe and you import a lot of your energy, uh all of a sudden Iran, but also previously the Russian gas being cut off, means that energy security is top of mind, and that helps quite a few of our holdings that help facilitate energy in Europe.
episode_title: Monthly Market Update - June 2026

headline: Property and infrastructure fund has added as a beneficiary of Middle East energy supply disruption
reasoning: Young highlights Cheniere Energy as a recent portfolio addition, describing it as a company that owns and operates LNG facilities on the US Gulf Coast. It takes natural gas piped in from the US, supercools it into LNG, and exports it by ship to Europe and Asia for industrial and power generation purposes. With approximately 20% of global oil and gas supply disrupted in the Middle East, Cheniere is well-positioned to benefit from the resulting increase in demand for US LNG exports.
quote: So, I'll call out Cheniere Energy, which is a company that owns and operates LNG facilities on the US Gulf Coast. So, they take natural gas that is piped in from the US, and they supercool it into liquid natural gas, LNG, and then that product is put on ships and exported to Europe and Asia. And there it's used for industrial purposes and power generation. So, they have benefited as about 20% of the world's oil and gas has been cut off in the Middle East.

headline: Pie Funds CIO sees 20-25% airport price declines as a buying opportunity, closing underweight and adding back exposure as long-term cash flows remain intact
reasoning: Taylor argues that airport cash flows over a 10-year horizon are highly predictable and will not be materially affected by the short-term Iran conflict. However, markets, which typically look only 3-6 months ahead, have driven airport share prices down 20-25% since the start of the conflict in late February. Taylor views this dislocation as an opportunity, noting the fund had been underweight airports through the conflict but has now closed that underweight and is buying back into airports at significantly cheaper prices, seeing the sell-off as a short-term event that does not affect long-term valuation.
quote: Infrastructure assets are incredibly stable. Um they're a great uh ballast to any um portfolio that a client might have. Uh a good example of actually how you can use an event like the Iran war um to take advantage of price fluctuations in these infrastructure assets. So, uh take for example an airport, uh the cash flows of an airport in 10 years time are reasonably predictable uh and likely to be pretty stable and won't won't really be impacted by what happens today. But of course, the market doesn't think like that. The market thinks 6 months ahead or 3 months ahead. Uh and many of the airport companies have seen their price fall 20 to 25% since the start of the conflict uh at the end of February. So, we we view that as an opportunity to um uh increase exposure to airports. We had been underweight once as Matt mentioned through the start of the conflict. Uh but actually just today uh we've closed that and looking to buy back into the airports that are now a lot cheaper than they were uh two two or three months ago just simply because of a short-term event which we don't think will affect the evaluation in 10 years.
episode_title: Monthly Market Update - June 2026
